claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch among constituent elements increases atomic-scale lattice distortion in high-entropy alloys.
Increased lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion enhances hardness and strength.
Alloy composition can be varied to change atomic size mismatch while phase stability, processing conditions, and microstructure remain constant.
Holding thermal and mechanical processing constant makes differences in hardness and strength attributable solely to lattice distortion.
Larger local lattice distortions act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The proposed barrier to dislocation motion is a solid-solution-strengthening mechanism.
Greater atomic size mismatch will produce statistically significant increases in hardness relative to a minimal-mismatch baseline.
Greater atomic size mismatch will produce statistically significant increases in yield strength relative to a minimal-mismatch baseline.
A baseline alloy with smaller atomic size differences will have lower lattice distortion.
A baseline alloy with lower lattice distortion will have lower hardness and strength.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold in single-phase high-entropy alloys when other strengthening mechanisms do not dominate.
Secondary-phase formation may cause deviations from the proposed relationship.
Non-ambient testing conditions may cause deviations from the proposed relationship.
The quantitative relationship between lattice distortion and mechanical properties may vary among alloy systems.
The quantitative relationship between lattice distortion and mechanical properties may vary with loading conditions.
